repos.title: SubRoformer: Subband Time-Domain Representation for Music Source Separation
repos.paper_summary: SubRoFormer is a Transformer-based music source separation system that splits a stereo mix into frequency-localized subbands, runs a separator on temporally compressed features, and predicts complex masks at 100 Hz. The subband module uses an overlapping triangular FIR filter bank, complex analytic conversion, baseband demodulation, and decimation, with a fast polyphase implementation. The separator combines a patched axial RoFormer (alternating subband-axis and temporal-axis attention with rotary embeddings) with a GEGLU gated residual fusion that merges coarse and fine-rate features. On MUSDB18-HQ, training only on that dataset, the target-specific models reach an average SDR of 10.63 dB across four stems, 0.61 dB above the strongest complete public-data BS-RoFormer result the authors report, and 0.99 dB above the reported Mel-RoFormer result. BS-RoFormer is 1.38 dB better on bass. With 500 extra training songs, a single multi-stem model reaches 11.59 dB. The subband transform alone reconstructs the mixture at 27.8 dB SDR-scale fidelity for mel and ERB banks, far below the near-perfect STFT and MDCT controls. The authors state the results are single-seed and directional, and that repeated seeds, efficiency measurements, and parameter-matched ablations are still needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Subband frontend plus a residual RoFormer separator targets the time-frequency trade-off in music source separation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior systems span waveform, hybrid, spectrogram, and subband separators, and the paper positions itself among them.

digest_headlines.heading: Subband Time-Domain Representation
digest_headlines.headline: A fixed triangular subband filter bank with polyphase implementation reconstructs the mixture with measured distortion.

digest_headlines.heading: Residual SubRoFormer
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer combines fine-rate features, a patched axial RoFormer, and gated residual fusion to predict complex masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use MUSDB18-HQ with SDR as the primary metric, and training data and augmentation are described.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer-B reaches 10.63 dB on MUSDB18-HQ without extra data, but the authors call the evidence preliminary.

repos.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
repos.paper_summary: PolicyIK is a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy that learns high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms through a joint-position interface. The policy accumulates its actions into a joint reference, observes that reference relative to the measured joints, and uses two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain. Its reward combines tracking, a running-best progress term, and a dwell term so the policy both reaches and holds a tolerance of 1 mm and 0.2°. In simulation on a 7-DoF arm, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps mean errors over the final second within tolerance on 93.5% of held-out tasks, rising to 98.9% with a deployment protocol. Ablations show each design choice lowers single-attempt success by 1.8 to 9.2 points when removed. On two physical arms, trained with FlashSAC, PolicyIK reaches and holds more tasks than four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, it executes the end-effector commands of the π0.5 VLA policy with 95.7% success across ten adapted LIBERO-Object tasks. Limitations: the policy's real-arm and pick-and-place results are reported with fewer detailed numbers in the text provided, and inference takes 0.035 ms on CPU against a 33 ms control period.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Policies that output end-effector poses inherit inverse kinematics accuracy, and precise inverse kinematics is hard to build.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior learned reaching controllers reach millimeter to centimeter accuracy, and sub-millimeter results need a classical solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Success is defined as mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2°, posed as goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method accumulates actions into a joint reference, scales them by error, and rewards each new best error and every step within tolerance.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: In simulation, one attempt reaches 93.5% strict success, rising to 98.9% with the deployment protocol.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Hardware training with the same terminal-phase design reaches and holds more tasks than all four classical controllers.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists simulation setup, reward and training settings, deployment protocol, baseline tuning, hardware controller settings, and xArm7 results.

repos.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
repos.paper_summary:
AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation policy trained on 16,151 hours of handheld-gripper demonstrations recorded with the open YUBI gripper, with no robot data collected. It builds on π0.5 and pre-trains with See Less, Specify More (S2), which adds a learned visual budget gate and language at task and subtask levels. Actions are gripper poses relative to the pose at observation time, so human and robot data share coordinates. Post-training adds stage prediction and proprioceptive memory.

On ten bimanual tasks run on a Franka at a site where no training data was recorded, A-0 averages 78% success over 15 trials per task. π0.5, XR-1, GR00T N1.7 and MolmoAct2, post-trained on the same demonstrations, average 27%, 23%, 16% and 14%, each at its best of a hyperparameter sweep. A-0 uses one recipe for all tasks. The same weights ran on TX-G2, OpenArm and UR on three or four tasks each, reported without success rates. Limitations: the quantitative results cover one platform, and the earbuds task reaches only 30%.

digest_headlines.heading: 1. Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: A-0 learns bimanual manipulation from 16,151 hours of handheld gripper demonstrations, with no robot data at any stage.

digest_headlines.heading: 2. Results
digest_headlines.headline: On ten tasks at an unseen site, A-0 averages 78% success and tops every task against four other models.

digest_headlines.heading: 3. Data
digest_headlines.headline: The corpus holds 16,151 hours of bimanual YUBI demonstrations split into 10.65 million subtask segments.

digest_headlines.heading: 4. Pre-training
digest_headlines.headline: Pre-training on more handheld data lowers post-training loss, each doubling cutting it by about 2.4%.

digest_headlines.heading: 5. Post-training
digest_headlines.headline: Post-training adds a stage head and a memory of the last ten states, and takes under four hours on eight H200 GPUs.

digest_headlines.heading: 6. Inference Harness
digest_headlines.headline: The harness smooths the predicted stage and decodes actions as a continuous stream with a non-uniform noise schedule.

digest_headlines.heading: 7. Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: A-0 builds on prior handheld collection and FlashVLA streaming, and adds no robot demonstrations.

digest_headlines.heading: 8. Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A-0 is the first system built on a corpus that is still growing, and it runs on robots carrying YUBI.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the post-training loss for each of the 16 task sets.

repos.title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
repos.paper_summary: TCSExam is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents across four theoretical computer science research tracks: theorem proving in Lean 4, solver engineering, explicit constructions, and open-conjecture prove-or-refute tasks. TCSExam-Full has 100 expert-reviewed tasks, and TCSExam-Lite has 20 tasks, five per track. Every submission is checked by the Lean kernel or an executable checker. Theorem and solver scores use per-attempt success and a Kimi K3-relative metric, and an aggregate TCSExam Index combines the tracks. On Full, GPT-6 Astra leads with an Index of 71.9 and a 70.0% complete-proof rate on 20 theorems without supplied lemmas. On Lite, Opus 5.5 leads with 72.3. Full and Lite rankings agree at Spearman ρ=0.93 across eight shared agents. Open-conjecture resolution is near zero for all agents, with the highest at 5.6% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on Full. The paper reports that solver submissions improved some public references and that one construction exceeded its task reference. Limitations: each track has only five to 30 tasks, and Lite uses a single attempt per task for most agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks cover parts of theoretical computer science, so TCSExam adds proofs, solvers, constructions, and open conjectures.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks cover proofs, solvers, or conjectures separately, and only TCSExam covers all four.

digest_headlines.heading: TCSExam
digest_headlines.headline: TCSExam assigns each task to one of four tracks, each with its own required output and success criterion.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Eight agents run on Full and nine on Lite, each attempt limited to a 12-hour development budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: GPT-6 Astra leads Full with an Index of 71.9, and Opus 5.5 leads Lite with 72.3.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The framework covers four research tracks, and Lite retains them while reducing attempts by 80%.

digest_headlines.heading: AI Use Statement
digest_headlines.headline: AI assistants helped author tasks, build checkers, and draft text, and the authors take responsibility for the content.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendices list the task catalogue, agent configurations, proof and solver details, and per-attempt results.

repos.title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
repos.paper_summary:
D3D is a standalone diffusion drafter for speculative decoding that does not need updated target-model hidden states, so the next draft block can be computed during target verification. It is initialized from a pretrained autoregressive model and trained on target-generated responses with blockwise denoising (block size 16) plus an auxiliary autoregressive loss. Layers are then pruned one at a time using validation acceptance length, with distillation-based recovery training. At inference, one packed drafter pass prepares continuations for possible rejection outcomes and full acceptance. A cache hit reuses a prepared branch; a miss triggers synchronous drafting.

On seven benchmarks with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, D3D averages 5.00× and 5.71× decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding. DFlash averages 4.03× and 3.67×, and DSpark averages 4.44× and 3.92×. The peak is 7.48× on GSM8K with Qwen3-32B. Average acceptance length at block size 16 is 7.88 (Qwen3-8B) and 7.73 (Qwen3-32B). Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks.

Limitations: the main comparison uses two GPUs (one for the target, one for the drafter), and per-GPU throughput is not compared. The drafter adds memory, cache misses stall verification, and experiments use the Transformers backend rather than SGLang or vLLM.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Target-conditioned drafters must wait for fresh target states, so drafting and verification run sequentially.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior drafters mostly condition on target features, whereas D3D trains without them and prunes layers.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: D3D trains a standalone drafter, prunes layers by acceptance loss, and prepares successor blocks during verification.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: D3D averages 5.00× and 5.71× decoding speedup, above DFlash's 4.03× and 3.67×, on seven benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors claim the first empirical demonstration of asynchronous lossless speculative decoding with a standalone diffusion drafter.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations are the extra drafter memory, synchronous drafting on cache misses, and no test in production serving frameworks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the teacher-adjustment formula, extra ablations on training weight, block size and anchors, and selective prefilling on LongBench.

repos.title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
repos.paper_summary: CompressionBench is a terminal task in which coding agents compress LLMs autonomously. Each agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, GPU, pinned runtime, and eight-hour budget, and must output compressed weights plus the inference code that runs them. Six agents each attempted six tasks (three source models, two storage limits each). Agents search using a perplexity-ratio reward. The frozen artifact is then verified on held-out likelihood, storage, and GSM8K, HumanEval, and TriviaQA accuracy, which must retain 80% of BF16. Of 36 submissions, 29 pass. The lowest-PPL passing artifact per task averages a 3.4% PPL increase over BF16 and 77.33% accuracy versus 79.56% for BF16. Agents lowered PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage. Complete-model feedback reversed 17 of 79 prior local rankings, and likelihood alone missed generation and execution failures. Limitations: each benchmark uses fifty questions, decode speed is excluded from the reward, and the link to recursive self-improvement, whether compressed models can perform later compression, is untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Compression becomes a terminal task: agents build compressed LLMs and inference code under a storage limit.

digest_headlines.heading: Compression as a Terminal Task
digest_headlines.headline: Verification scores only models that fit both storage limits and retain 80% of BF16 accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Study
digest_headlines.headline: Twenty-nine of thirty-six agent-built models pass verification, and the best per task averages a 3.4% perplexity increase.

digest_headlines.heading: How Agents Improve Compression
digest_headlines.headline: At nearly fixed storage, agents lowered perplexity in 21 of 24 revisions by refining quantizers or precision.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work supplies agent benchmarks and compression methods; this paper combines them into one agent-built model task.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agent compression needs numerical design, experimental judgment, and validation; whether compressed models retain this ability is untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists evaluation protocol, search stopping, full measurements, pilot storage studies, and controlled ablations.

repos.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
repos.paper_summary: Library of Layers (LoL) is a transformer architecture in which a small router selects, for each window of tokens at each depth, one block from a shared library of layers, so the execution order is chosen at inference. Library size is the single knob: a small library forces parameter reuse (as in looped models) and a large library leaves blocks idle (as in mixture-of-experts models). Attention is strided window attention, with windows shifted between depths so information crosses window boundaries while causality is kept. On synthetic sudoku and maze tasks, forcing a router path for a given strategy produces that strategy with close to 100% accuracy. The router's routing features reach 0.920 AUROC on a held-out safe/unsafe test set using a linear probe, and 0.950 with sequence-level averaging. At 360M parameters, LoL is compared with looped transformers using training loss over FLOPs averaged over 3 seeds. At 1B parameters on math data, LoL stays within 2 standard errors of the vanilla and sliding-window baselines on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and GSM8K. Limitations: the sudoku and maze results use synthetic data, the 1B benchmark differences are mostly within error bars, and the paper calls itself an initial exploration.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed layer order limits transformers, so the paper proposes a router that picks each next layer from a shared library.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior looped, skipping and mixture-of-experts designs keep layer order or parameter choices fixed, while LoL selects whole blocks per window.

digest_headlines.heading: How to Learn the Order of a Forward Pass
digest_headlines.headline: Each window selects one library block per depth; shifted window boundaries keep attention causal, and depth grows during training.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Learned routing paths separate languages and algorithms, and LoL stays competitive with dense, looped and mixture-of-experts baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors call this an initial exploration and propose controllability, test-time scaling and adapter routing as next steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists architecture and training details, ablations, extra benchmark tables, sudoku and maze data, and routing visualizations.

repos.title: ARLoop: Fully-Open Pre-trained Looped Transformers with Attention Residuals
repos.paper_summary: ARLoop applies attention residuals to looped transformers, so each sublayer learns to weight earlier residual blocks instead of summing all prior updates with fixed unit weights. Sublayers are grouped into blocks, and a sliding-window variant keeps the input embedding plus the three most recent blocks. In controlled runs on 140M and 370M decoder-only models trained on FineWeb-Edu (11.2B and 29.6B tokens), ARLoop reaches the lowest validation perplexity among the compared residual designs, including PreNorm, Sandwich Norm, DeepLoop, and Parcae. At 140M with R=5, it scores 15.84 against 16.34 for PreNormLoop. At 370M with R=3, it scores 12.17 against 12.48. Sliding-window attention matches full-history attention at R=2 and gives lower perplexity at deeper recurrences. The authors also train 0.6B and 1.2B models under a larger pretraining recipe. The 1.2B model, trained on 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B on all evaluated tasks and is described as competitive with Qwen3.5-2B. Against PreNorm, the paper reports +5.2 points on GSM8K and +3.1 on MBPP. Limitations: on a single H100 at R=4, full-history attention runs about 15% slower than PreNorm and sliding-window attention about 10% slower. Performance does not improve beyond the maximum training recurrence at inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Standard residuals cannot select earlier looped representations, so ARLoop applies attention over depth to each sublayer.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior looped models release little training detail, and residual designs were rarely tested on math and coding.

digest_headlines.heading: ARLoop
digest_headlines.headline: Attention residuals weight each earlier residual source, and block grouping with a sliding window cuts the sources each sublayer reads.

digest_headlines.heading: Controlled Evaluation of ARLoop
digest_headlines.headline: ARLoop gives the lowest validation perplexity among tested residual designs, and sliding windows match full-history attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling to Practical Pretraining of Looped Transformers
digest_headlines.headline: ARLoop-0.6B beats PreNormLoop on seven of eight tasks, and ARLoop-1.2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-2B on all eight.

digest_headlines.heading: Further discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed recurrence beat dynamic recurrence, and extra recurrences beyond training depth gave no further perplexity gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Across controlled and pretraining experiments, selective residual access helped looped transformers use recurrent depth.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers architecture, training, value residuals, ablations, per-task results, baseline formulas, and extrapolation details.

repos.title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design
repos.paper_summary: FastAgent is a campaign controller for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) that chooses, for each quantity of interest (QoI), the physical model, grid and time-step resolution, simulation horizon, and which candidates to escalate to Fluent. It runs on FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine that returns fields, QoIs and cost estimates for rapid screening. Returned Fluent discrepancies update candidate ranking and later fidelity choices. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, relative to a matched Generic Agent control, it reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68–99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53–15.36. In high-pressure steam dewaxing for investment casting, the rapid route locates the risk window with 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference, while Fluent confirms melt completion. After screening 131,072 outlet layouts and evaluating selected candidates with Fluent and Abaqus, the authors identify Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. Limitations: the only agent baseline is the Generic Agent control, the fast route's full-melt error was 12.1%, and the dewaxing and fracture results are simulation-based.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: FastAgent couples a rapid physics engine with QoI-aware fidelity control and discrepancy feedback for industrial CFD campaigns.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Across six public benchmark campaigns, FastAgent cut worst-QoI error by 5.68–99.14% and accelerated computation by factors of 1.53–15.36 versus a Generic Agent control.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: The methods define the campaign policy, FastFluent governing formulations, error metrics and fracture-based layout screening.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: FastAgent identifies Sparse-6, which cuts simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% versus the Original design.

digest_headlines.heading: Data availability
digest_headlines.headline: Supporting data are in the Article and Supplementary Information, while industrial geometries and proprietary process data are confidential.

digest_headlines.heading: Code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The FastFluent code and agent workflow are openly available in a GitHub repository.

digest_headlines.heading: Competing interests
digest_headlines.headline: The authors declare no competing interests.

repos.title: VLM-as-a-Judge for Person Re-Identification
repos.paper_summary:
This paper proposes a training-free ensemble for cloth-changing person re-identification. Two frozen experts, DIFFER and SapiensID, each retrieve gallery matches, and a frozen general-purpose VLM (Qwen3.6-27B) reorders the merged top-k candidates zero-shot. The VLM is invoked only on queries where the two experts disagree at rank 1. On CHIRLA's four scenarios, the merged pool of 16 reaches 64.4 average rank-1, against 51.4 for SapiensID, the better expert, and 55.0 for the best naive ensemble (score fusion). Both gaps are significant. Merging the experts' shortlists matches or beats reranking SapiensID's list alone at lower cost, though the advantage is only resolved at a pool size of 6. Gating removes 40% of judge calls and 35% of compute with no significant rank-1 change, at a cost of 1.8 to 3.8 mAP points.

The evaluation rests on CHIRLA's 22 identities, so the disagreement rate and the savings may differ on other data. The judge is order-sensitive and sometimes groups candidates by coarse attributes such as apparent gender. Reranking remains the dominant cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Two CC-ReID experts make different errors, so a VLM judge over their merged shortlists could help.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work uses language in training or as a standalone matcher, not as an arbiter over expert shortlists.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Training-free arbitration: a VLM reranks the union of candidates only where the two experts' rank-1 identities disagree.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The gated VLM judge raises average rank-1 by 12.9 points over SapiensID on CHIRLA's four scenarios.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: Gating removes 40% of judge calls for a 1.8 to 3.8 mAP cost, and the results rest on CHIRLA's 22 identities.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The acknowledgments thank collaborators and list funding sources, and the authors declare no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, FLOPs calculation, ensemble baselines, full pool-budget results, uncertainty estimates, prompt templates, and tail-rule ablation.
